Captured at vision walk #4 (2026-04-27) following operator rejection of dec-1777232229870857566. These principles extend STRATEGY.md voice canon and become the contract for future dev-log drafts (oss-advertiser primary; subscription-advertiser when applicable). All future dev-log drafts must satisfy them.

PRINCIPLES:

1. ESSAY-SHAPE PER POST. Each dev-log post (thread, blog, video) has hook → introduction → body → conclusion. Not a list of atomic items, not a changelog. The reader must finish with a reason to come back, click the profile, find the others. The 3-7-tweets-per-thread guidance in STRATEGY.md content-type principles needs to be read as 'a thread is a single essay split across tweets,' not 'a thread is N atomic tweets.'

2. INTRODUCTION ON FIRST MENTION. Before referring to any scenario, agent, or internal concept by name in published material, check shared/published-scenario-mentions.jsonl. If the subject has not been published before, the post must briefly introduce it: what it is, why it exists, what it does at a one-sentence level. After first publish, subsequent posts may use a one-line refresher ('swarm-manager — the agent-orchestration substrate') instead of a full intro. First-ever dev-log carries an outsized intro burden because every concept is new to the audience.

3. PERSONAL VOICE GROUNDED IN BUILDER IDENTITY. STRATEGY.md says 'first person, conversational, technically credible.' This needs to be embodied, not just stated. The first post in a series especially must feel like a software engineer talking about what they built — real grounded excitement, real hype tied to real work, not corporate-changelog third-person. 'Here's what I've been working on…' lands harder than 'swarm-manager just shipped.' The 'I' can be the operator's or an agent's — pick deliberately, but pick.

4. WHAT → WHY FRAMING. Every change shown must carry its own reason-to-care. 'resolve.go is 52 lines + 202 test lines' is what. 'so an initiative dispatches work to whichever agent the scenario expects, instead of hard-coding the wire' is why. The why should connect to broader narrative — last post's setup, next post's payoff, the project's vision. Show only changes that actually matter; do not narrate every commit. Use shared/published-improvements-log.jsonl to track what has already been narrated per scenario, so the next post advances the story rather than repeating it.

5. HOOK-vs-BODY CHAR-COUNT ASYMMETRY. X allows long posts now with show-more gating. The first / hook tweet should be short to grab attention (<280 chars feels right). Body tweets should carry the actual substance and may be longer when needed. Do not enforce a uniform char limit across every tweet — that strips substance from body tweets without buying anything in the hook. Track lengths but apply the cap position-aware.

6. INTER-POST LINKAGE. Each post in a series must connect to its predecessor. Mechanism: previous_post_url stored in publish-log.jsonl after operator pastes the URL back; cited in the new post's last reply or visible link. Readers landing on the new post can find the prior chain. Without this, every post is an island.

7. NO INTERNAL NUMBERING. Internal artifacts (p8, round-002, milestone-3) are operational vocabulary — they do not belong externally. The only sequential numbering that goes outside is the dev-log post number itself (post #1, post #7), which signals to readers there are others to find. If internal pass numbers are mentioned externally, the audience cannot place them in any narrative they have access to.

8. SUBJECT FAMILIARITY MATTERS. Acceptable hooks for an audience that knows swarm-manager are not acceptable hooks for an audience that does not. Anti-pattern: hook assumes 'swarm-manager' is shared vocabulary on first publish. Pattern: hook either introduces the subject before the click-through, or hangs the click-through on a more universal frame (a problem, a question, a story) that the introduction follows.
